    All in One View

    Content from 1. Introduction to genetic variation and variant calling

    Last updated on 2026-10-11 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 50 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What kinds of genetic variation can short-read sequencing detect?
    • How does a variant caller turn aligned reads into a genotype?
    • Why can a variant call be wrong?
    • What question will we answer with the Ashkenazi trio today?

    Objectives

    • Distinguish SNVs, MNVs, indels and SVs/CNVs, and germline from somatic variants.
    • Read diploid genotypes (0/0, 0/1, 1/1, ./.).
    • Explain how a call is inferred from read evidence and base and mapping quality, and why errors arise.
    • Describe the workflow and its files.
    • State the workshop question for the GIAB Ashkenazi trio (HG002, HG003, HG004).

    Introduction

    Variant calling answers a simple-sounding question: where does the DNA of this individual differ from a reference sequence, and what are the two alleles at each of those positions? The answer is never read directly off the sequencer. It is inferred from millions of short, imperfect reads, each placed on the genome by an aligner that can also be wrong. Every call is therefore a statistical statement with a confidence attached, and part of the job is deciding which statements to believe.

    In this workshop we call variants on chromosome 20 in three people: a child and both parents, from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Ashkenazi trio. Their genomes have been characterized so thoroughly that public benchmark call sets exist for all three, so later in the day we can measure how many of our calls are right instead of guessing.

    This episode introduces the vocabulary and the reasoning. There are no commands to run.

    Types of genetic variation

    A variant is a position, or a stretch of sequence, where a sample differs from the reference genome. The allele that matches the reference is the reference allele (REF); any other allele is an alternate allele (ALT).

    Type What changes Example (reference > sample)
    Single-nucleotide variant (SNV) One base is replaced by another T > C
    Multi-nucleotide variant (MNV) Two or more adjacent bases change together AG > TC
    Insertion or deletion (indel) Bases are added or removed T > TTGG (insertion), CAT > C (deletion)
    Structural variant (SV) Larger rearrangements: large deletions and insertions, inversions, translocations thousands of bases moved or lost
    Copy-number variant (CNV) A segment is present in more or fewer copies than in the reference a gene present three times instead of twice

    In this lesson, “small variants” means SNVs and indels shorter than 50 bp. Structural and copy-number variants need different methods and are not covered (see the setup page).

    SNVs come in two kinds that matter later. A transition exchanges a purine for a purine (A and G) or a pyrimidine for a pyrimidine (C and T). A transversion exchanges a purine for a pyrimidine or the reverse. The ratio of the two (Ts/Tv) is a quick quality check on a call set, which Episode 6 uses.

    Germline and somatic variants

    A germline variant was inherited from a parent or arose in a parent’s egg or sperm, so it is present in every cell of the body. A somatic variant arose after conception, in some cells only, and is present in only a fraction of the cells sampled. A germline variant in a diploid individual is therefore expected in either half of the reads (one copy) or all of them (two copies). A somatic variant can be present in any fraction. This workshop calls germline variants; somatic calling uses different statistical models and is not covered.

    A de novo variant is a germline variant present in a child and absent from both parents. They are rare, and Episode 8 will show how hard they are to find among the many apparent de novo calls that are errors.

    The reference is a coordinate system

    The reference genome is one haploid sequence used as a shared map. Every position has a name (chr20:88108 is base 88,108 of chromosome 20), and REF is simply the base found at that position in the reference. REF is not “normal”, “healthy” or “ancestral”, and ALT is not necessarily rare or harmful. An ALT allele only differs from the reference sequence; it can be the more common allele at that position in many populations.

    Callout

    Two different frequencies

    Two numbers are easy to confuse:

    • Variant allele fraction (within one sample): the fraction of reads at a position that carry the ALT allele, for example 18 of 40 reads, 0.45. It tells you about the genotype of that one sample.
    • Population allele frequency: the fraction of chromosomes in a population that carry the ALT allele, for example from gnomAD (Episode 7). It tells you how common the allele is among other people.

    A heterozygous call has an allele fraction near 0.5 whether the allele is rare or common in the population.

    Diploid genotypes

    Humans are diploid: each autosome is present in two copies, one from each parent. A genotype lists the two alleles at a position, written as allele numbers: 0 is REF, 1 is the first ALT, 2 the second ALT, and so on. This is how genotypes appear in a VCF file, the format Episode 5A produces (VCF specification).

    Genotype Name Meaning
    0/0 homozygous reference both copies match the reference
    0/1 heterozygous one copy REF, one copy ALT
    1/1 homozygous alternate both copies carry the ALT allele
    1/2 heterozygous, two ALT alleles each copy carries a different ALT allele
    ./. missing no genotype could be called (for example, no reads)

    The / means the two alleles are unphased: we know which two alleles are present, not which parental chromosome carries which. A | (as in 0|1) marks a phased genotype.

    From reads to a genotype

    A caller sees, at each position, the stack of aligned reads covering it: the pileup. The schematic pileups below show a 9 bp window. Dots are bases that match the reference; letters are mismatches.

    SCHEMATIC, NOT DATA
position     1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
reference    A C G T T G C A T
read 1       . . . . C . . . .
read 2       . . . . . . . . .
read 3       . . . . C . . . .
read 4       . . . . . . . . .
read 5       . . . . C . . . .
read 6       . . . . . . . . .
read 7       . . . . C . . . .
read 8       . . . . . . . . .

    At position 5, four of eight reads carry C and four carry the reference T. That is what a heterozygous T/C (genotype 0/1) is expected to look like. A homozygous ALT site would show C in nearly every read.

    Not every read counts equally. Two kinds of quality decide how much a read contributes:

    • Base quality is the sequencer’s estimate that a base call is wrong, on the Phred scale: Q = -10 log10(probability of error). Q20 means a 1 in 100 chance of error, Q30 1 in 1,000 (SAM specification). A mismatch on a Q2 base is weak evidence; a mismatch on a Q37 base is strong evidence.
    • Mapping quality (MAPQ) is the aligner’s estimate, on the same scale, that the read is placed at the wrong position in the genome. A read from a repeat that occurs twice in the genome cannot be placed with confidence, and gets a mapping quality near 0 (Episode 4).

    The caller then asks, for each possible genotype (0/0, 0/1, 1/1): how likely are these reads, with these qualities, if that genotype were true? Those genotype likelihoods are stored in the VCF as PL, Phred-scaled so that the most likely genotype gets 0. The called genotype is the most probable one, and two quality values summarize the confidence (VCF specification; bcftools manual):

    • QUAL, per site: how confident the caller is that any ALT allele is present at this position in any of the samples.
    • GQ (genotype quality), per sample: how confident the caller is that this sample’s genotype is the right one.

    Calling, filtering and interpretation are separate steps. The caller writes down every site it thinks may be variant, together with these qualities. Filtering (Episode 6) decides which calls to trust. Interpretation (Episodes 7 and 8) decides what the trusted calls mean. Mixing them up, for example by treating every line of a raw VCF as a real variant, is one of the most common errors in variant analysis.

    Animation placeholder: “From reads to a genotype” (about 80 seconds) goes here. Its storyboard, scene list and alt text are specified in maintenance/plan/figures/reads-to-genotype.md (local file, not published); P7 builds the HTML animation in the style of the RNA-seq lesson animations. Until then, draw the pileup above on the board and walk through the three genotype hypotheses.

    Challenge

    Challenge: call the genotype

    Each schematic pileup shows one position in one sample. All bases have high base quality, and all reads have high mapping quality unless marked. What genotype would you call at the marked position (*), and how confident are you?

    SCHEMATIC, NOT DATA        position *, reference base G

Pileup A (10 reads)   G G A G A A G A G A
Pileup B (3 reads)    A A A
Pileup C (12 reads)   A A A A A A A A A A A A
Pileup D (10 reads)   G G G G G G G G G A
Pileup E (8 reads)    A A A A G G G G     (every read has mapping quality 0)
    • A: 5 A and 5 G: heterozygous 0/1, called with confidence.
    • B: 3 A: most likely 1/1, but only three reads. A heterozygous site shows only one allele in three reads one time in four (next section), so the genotype quality is low.
    • C: 12 A: homozygous alternate 1/1, confident.
    • D: one A in 10 reads: most likely 0/0 with one sequencing error. If the A had low base quality, even more so.
    • E: the allele fraction looks like a perfect heterozygote, but every read has mapping quality 0. The reads may come from another copy of a repeat, so the “variant” may be a difference between two copies of the repeat, not between this person’s two chromosomes. A careful caller gives it little or no weight. Episode 6 filters sites like this on mapping quality.

    How many reads make a heterozygous call?

    At a heterozygous site, each read comes from one of the two chromosomes with equal probability, like a coin toss. With n reads, the chance that all of them come from the same chromosome, so that the site looks homozygous, is 2 x 0.5^n. This idealized model ignores sequencing errors and assumes both chromosomes are sampled equally.

    Reads (n) Chance a heterozygous site shows only one allele
    3 0.25 (1 in 4)
    5 0.0625 (1 in 16)
    10 0.002 (about 1 in 500)
    15 0.00006 (about 1 in 16,000)
    Challenge

    Challenge: how many reads before you trust a heterozygous call?

    1. Use the formula above. At 5 reads, how often would a true heterozygous site look homozygous? At 10 reads?
    2. Our samples have a mean depth of about 39x on chromosome 20 (Episode 4). Why is the mean depth not enough to say that every heterozygous site will be called correctly?
    3. In Episode 6 we will set genotypes supported by fewer than 10 reads to missing (./.). What do we gain, and what do we lose?
    1. At 5 reads, 2 x 0.5^5 = 0.0625, about one heterozygous site in 16 looks homozygous. At 10 reads, 2 x 0.5^10 = 0.002, about one in 500. The benchmark for the child alone lists more than 70,000 SNVs on chromosome 20 (Episode 6), so even one in 500 of the heterozygous ones adds up.
    2. Depth varies along the genome. A mean of 39x includes positions with far fewer reads (and far more), and the low-depth positions are where heterozygous sites are missed or miscalled. Episode 4 measures how much of chromosome 20 is covered at a given depth.
    3. We gain precision: genotypes with too little evidence no longer count as calls. We lose recall: some true genotypes become missing. Episode 6 measures this trade-off against the benchmark.

    Why calls can be wrong

    Every error source below produces calls that look real in a raw VCF:

    • Sequencing errors. A wrong base on a few reads looks like a low-fraction ALT allele. Base quality and the number of supporting reads separate most of them from real variants.
    • Sampling. Too few reads, or unlucky sampling, makes a heterozygous site look homozygous or hides it (previous section).
    • Mapping errors. Reads from a repeat or a duplicated region can be placed at the wrong copy. Differences between the copies then look like variants. Mapping quality flags many of these reads, not all.
    • Duplicates. Copies of the same original DNA fragment are not independent evidence. Episode 4 marks them so the caller can skip them.
    • Reference problems. Gaps, errors or collapsed repeats in the reference attract misplaced reads.
    • Representation. One indel can often be written in several equivalent ways, and two call sets can disagree only in how they wrote it. Episode 5A normalizes calls to remove this.

    What short reads cannot see

    Our reads are 151 bases long, from DNA fragments a few hundred bases long. A read cannot be placed uniquely if it falls entirely inside a repeat longer than the fragment. In our data, about 5% of each sample’s reads get mapping quality 0, which means the aligner found several equally good places for them (Episode 4).

    Repeats concentrate the errors. In the reference run of this workshop, the centromere of chromosome 20, about 5.6% of the chromosome’s length, held 22% of the raw SNV calls in the child (HG002), with a transition/transversion ratio of 1.22, far below the 2.28 of calls inside the benchmark regions (reference-run memo, section 3). Many of those calls are almost certainly mapping artifacts, and Episode 6 filters most of them.

    Short reads also miss most structural variants, cannot resolve which copy of a segmental duplication a read comes from, and cannot tell which parental chromosome carries each allele over long distances (phasing). Other methods, such as long-read sequencing, are needed for these questions; they are outside the scope of this workshop.

    The workflow and its files

    Step Episode Tools Input Output
    Set up the project and check the data 2 rsync, md5sum, samtools staged copy on Depot data/, ref/, resources/, scripts/, results/
    Check read quality 3 FastQC, MultiQC FASTQ (data/*.fastq.gz) results/qc/multiqc_report.html
    Align reads, mark duplicates 4 bwa mem, samtools FASTQ, reference and bwa index results/bam/<sample>.markdup.bam and .csi index
    Check the alignments 4 samtools, mosdepth, MultiQC BAM results/qc_alignment/
    Call variants jointly in the trio 5A bcftools three BAMs, reference results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz
    Filter and evaluate 6 bcftools, hap.py VCF, GIAB benchmarks results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz, results/eval/
    Annotate 7 SnpEff, bcftools filtered VCF, gnomAD frequencies results/annot/trio.ann.vcf.gz
    Find candidate variants in the trio 8 bcftools annotated VCF, PED file results/trio/funnel.tsv, results/trio/candidates.tsv

    The file formats (FASTQ, BAM, VCF, BED, PED) are introduced in the episode where they first appear.

    A workflow diagram for this table is a P7 figure (plan section 2). Until it exists, sketch the boxes on the board: FASTQ to BAM to VCF, with the QC step after each.

    The workshop question

    The trio is a child (HG002) and both parents (HG003, HG004). By the end of the day we will ask:

    In the child, which variants are consistent with a de novo or a recessive inheritance model, are plausibly protein-altering, and are rare in an ancestry-matched population? How many of these candidates survive inspection?

    Answering it needs every step of the workflow: good alignments, trustworthy calls, filters we can justify, measured error rates, and annotation. It also needs restraint. These are public reference samples, and nothing we find says anything about anyone’s health. The goal is to learn how evidence accumulates, and how often an exciting-looking candidate turns out to be an error.

    Discussion

    Discussion: what would convince you?

    Suppose the final list contains one variant that is heterozygous in the child and absent from both parents. Before calling it a de novo mutation, what evidence would you want to see? Keep your list; Episode 8 comes back to it.

    Summary

    Key Points
    • A variant is a difference from the reference sequence. The reference is a coordinate system, not a description of a healthy or ancestral genome.
    • Diploid genotypes are written as allele numbers: 0/0, 0/1, 1/1, and ./. for missing.
    • A caller weighs each read by its base quality and mapping quality, computes genotype likelihoods, and reports the most probable genotype with QUAL and GQ.
    • At a heterozygous site, the chance of seeing only one allele in n reads is 2 x 0.5^n, so low-depth genotypes are unreliable.
    • Sequencing errors, sampling, mapping errors in repeats, duplicates and representation differences all produce calls that look real. Calling, filtering and interpretation are separate steps.

    Content from 2. Data, reference genomes, and project setup

    Last updated on 2026-10-11 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 40 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What data will we analyze, and where does it come from?
    • What makes a reference genome suitable for variant calling?
    • How do we organize the project and record sample metadata?
    • How do we check that the data is complete and unchanged?

    Objectives

    • Verify the staged copy and lay out the project.
    • Describe the HG002, HG003 and HG004 trio and record its metadata as a sample sheet and a PED file.
    • Explain the GRCh38 no-alt analysis set, contig naming and index files (.fai, .dict, aligner index).
    • Convert BED (0-based, half-open) to VCF-style (1-based) coordinates.
    • Check integrity with md5.

    Introduction

    Before any analysis, we need to know exactly what the data is, where it came from, and that our copy is complete. In this episode we look at the dataset and its sample metadata, check the files with checksums, and get to know the reference genome and its index files. These are short steps, but most failed variant-calling runs trace back to one of them: a truncated file, a reference that does not match the reads, or a sample recorded under the wrong name.

    Prerequisite

    Before you start

    Complete the “Data setup” section of the setup page: copy the workshop data to $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop and link the reference into ref/. Every command in this episode runs on a Negishi login node; they are all quick.

    The Ashkenazi trio

    The Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) consortium, hosted by NIST, characterizes reference human genomes and publishes benchmark variant calls for them. We use its Ashkenazi trio, a son and his parents:

    Sample Cell line Role Sex
    HG002 NA24385 child male
    HG003 NA24149 father male
    HG004 NA24143 mother female

    The reads come from the DeepTrio WGS case study, which provides alignments of each sample to GRCh38 restricted to chromosome 20. We converted those alignments back to paired FASTQ files, so that you can align them yourself. The facts below were measured on the source files in this workshop’s feasibility run (feasibility memo):

    • Sequencing: Illumina NovaSeq, PCR-free library, 151 bp paired-end reads.
    • Base qualities: binned to four values (Episode 3).
    • Depth: the files are labeled 35x, but the mean depth on chromosome 20 is about 40x (39.2x to 39.9x in the source alignments).
    • Duplicates: the source alignments had duplicates marked, not removed (about 2.0 million flagged reads per sample). Converting to FASTQ kept those reads, so you will mark duplicates again in Episode 4.
    • Read pairs: HG002 9,462,450, HG003 9,480,040, HG004 9,347,118. All six FASTQ files together are 4.85 GB.
    Callout

    The reads were selected from chromosome 20 alignments

    Every read in our FASTQ files was aligned to chromosome 20 in the source data. About 330,000 reads per sample had a mate aligned elsewhere in the genome, and those reads were dropped, because a read without its mate cannot go into a paired FASTQ file.

    Two consequences follow. First, when we align these reads to the whole genome in Episode 4, almost all of them land on chromosome 20 again. Mapping rates near 100% and almost no coverage on other chromosomes are artifacts of how the data was selected, not properties of a real whole-genome run. Second, reads that the source alignment placed on other chromosomes were never selected, so this data cannot show reads moving between chromosome 20 and similar sequences elsewhere, as they would in a real whole-genome run.

    Project layout

    The setup page created this layout under $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop:

    Directory Contents
    data/ the six FASTQ files, md5sums.txt, the sample sheet samples.tsv, the pedigree trio.ped
    ref/ links to the read-only reference genome, its indexes and the annotation database on Depot
    resources/ benchmark call sets (truth/), population frequencies (gnomad/), region lists (regions/), and a small example VCF (example/)
    scripts/ the SLURM job scripts for Episodes 4 to 7
    results/ one folder per step: qc, bam, qc_alignment, vcf, eval, annot, trio

    The reference and its indexes take more than 10 GB. Every learner uses the same files, so they stay in one read-only copy on Depot, and ref/ holds symbolic links to them instead of copies.

    Step 1: Check the copy with checksums

    A checksum is a short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents. If a single byte changes, the checksum changes. md5sums.txt holds the MD5 checksum of every FASTQ file as it was staged; md5sum -c recomputes each one and compares.

    BASH 

    cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop

    BASH 

    cd data
md5sum -c md5sums.txt
cd ..

    This reads all 4.85 GB, so give it up to a minute.

    OUTPUT 

    HG002_R1.fastq.gz: OK
HG002_R2.fastq.gz: OK
HG003_R1.fastq.gz: OK
HG003_R2.fastq.gz: OK
HG004_R1.fastq.gz: OK
HG004_R2.fastq.gz: OK

    Every file must report OK. A FAILED line means that file is damaged or incomplete; copy it again with the rsync command from the setup page and rerun the check.

    Callout

    Why checksums?

    File sizes can match while contents differ, and a transfer that stops early can leave a file that looks normal until a tool fails on it hours later. Checksums catch both. Record them when you receive data, check them after every copy, and keep them with the data as part of its provenance. The sources we downloaded from publish checksums too, and we checked every download against them before staging (data-prep/sources.tsv lists each file, its size and its MD5).

    Step 2: The sample sheet and the pedigree

    Two small text files describe the samples. Every later step reads them, so they are worth a careful look.

    BASH 

    head data/samples.tsv
cat data/trio.ped

    OUTPUT 

    sample	role	sex	family	fastq_r1	fastq_r2	rg_id	rg_lb	rg_pl
HG002	child	1	AJ	HG002_R1.fastq.gz	HG002_R2.fastq.gz	HG002.pcr-free	HG002.pcr-free	ILLUMINA
HG003	father	1	AJ	HG003_R1.fastq.gz	HG003_R2.fastq.gz	HG003.pcr-free	HG003.pcr-free	ILLUMINA
HG004	mother	2	AJ	HG004_R1.fastq.gz	HG004_R2.fastq.gz	HG004.pcr-free	HG004.pcr-free	ILLUMINA
AJ	HG002	HG003	HG004	1	0
AJ	HG003	0	0	1	0
AJ	HG004	0	0	2	0

    samples.tsv is the sample sheet: one row per sample, with a header. Its columns are the sample name, its role and sex, the family, the two FASTQ files, and three read-group fields (rg_id, rg_lb, rg_pl) that Episode 4 writes into the alignments. The alignment script reads it line by line, so the sample names in the VCF come from this file.

    trio.ped is a pedigree file in the PED format used by PLINK, bcftools and other tools (PLINK file formats). It has no header and six whitespace-separated columns:

    1. family ID
    2. individual ID
    3. father’s ID (0 if not in the file)
    4. mother’s ID (0 if not in the file)
    5. sex (1 male, 2 female, 0 unknown)
    6. phenotype (1 unaffected, 2 affected, 0 or -9 missing)

    The parents have 0 in columns 3 and 4 because their own parents are not part of the dataset. No phenotype is recorded for anyone. Episode 8 uses this file to check Mendelian inheritance.

    Challenge

    Challenge: write a PED line

    1. Without looking at trio.ped, write the PED line for HG002. Then compare it with the file.
    2. Suppose the family had a second child, a daughter with the sample ID KID2, sequenced in the same project. Write her line.
    3. What would go wrong in a trio analysis if columns 3 and 4 of HG002’s line were swapped?

    1. The family ID in this file is AJ, and HG002 is male with no recorded phenotype:

      AJ	HG002	HG003	HG004	1	0

      It should match the first line of trio.ped shown above.

    2. AJ KID2 HG003 HG004 2 0: same family, same parents, sex 2 for female.

    3. Swapping father and mother changes nothing for autosomal inheritance checks such as the ones in Episode 8, but any analysis that uses sex, for example of the X chromosome, would treat the father as the mother. Metadata errors rarely fail loudly; check this file whenever you build one.

    Step 3: The reference genome

    We align to GRCh38, the current human reference assembly, in a version prepared for read-alignment pipelines: the no-alt analysis set from NCBI (README in the NCBI directory). According to its README, it contains:

    • the chromosomes, the mitochondrial genome, and the unlocalized and unplaced scaffolds of GRCh38;
    • an Epstein-Barr virus sequence (chrEBV), not part of the human genome, included as a “sink” for reads from the virus, which are often present in sequencing samples;
    • and it leaves out the alternate locus scaffolds (alt contigs), extra versions of highly variable regions, because many alignment pipelines cannot handle them. An aligner that is not alt-aware would split reads from those regions between near-identical copies and give them low mapping quality (bwa README-alt).

    The README also states that the two pseudoautosomal regions on chromosome Y, and duplicate copies of some centromeric arrays, are masked with N, for the same reason. Our copy has no decoy sequences (the README describes a separate set with them).

    Callout

    Why the exact reference matters

    Reads, alignments, variant calls, benchmarks and annotation databases must all use the same assembly and the same sequence names. GRCh37 and GRCh38 coordinates differ. Even within GRCh38, sequence names differ between sources: this analysis set uses UCSC-style names (chr20), while some other resources name the same sequence 20. A mismatch rarely fails loudly. More often a tool silently finds no overlap, or skips the “unknown” chromosome, and the result is empty or wrong. Check names first whenever you combine files from different sources.

    The reference comes with index files. Each tool needs its own:

    File Made by Used by What it holds
    GRCh38_no_alt.fa.fai samtools faidx samtools, bcftools, most tools name, length and byte offsets of each sequence, for fast random access
    GRCh38_no_alt.dict samtools dict GATK and Picard (Episode 5B) a sequence dictionary: names, lengths and MD5 checksums in SAM header format
    GRCh38_no_alt.fa.{amb,ann,bwt,pac,sa} bwa index bwa (Episode 4) the aligner’s index; NCBI publishes it, so we did not build it
    GRCh38_no_alt.sdf rtg format hap.py with the vcfeval engine (Episode 6) the reference in RTG’s format

    Look at the FASTA index and the dictionary:

    BASH 

    head -3 ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa.fai
grep -w chr20 ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa.fai
wc -l ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa.fai
head -3 ref/GRCh38_no_alt.dict

    OUTPUT 

    chr1	248956422	112	70	71
chr2	242193529	252513167	70	71
chr3	198295559	498166716	70	71
chr20	64444167	2751788762	70	71
195 ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa.fai
@HD	VN:1.0	SO:unsorted
@SQ	SN:chr1	LN:248956422	M5:6aef897c3d6ff0c78aff06ac189178dd	UR:GRCh38_no_alt.fa	AS:GRCh38	SP:Homo sapiens
@SQ	SN:chr2	LN:242193529	M5:f98db672eb0993dcfdabafe2a882905c	UR:GRCh38_no_alt.fa	AS:GRCh38	SP:Homo sapiens

    The .fai columns are the sequence name, its length, the byte offset of its first base in the FASTA file, the number of bases per line, and the number of bytes per line. The analysis set has 195 sequences. chr20 is 64,444,167 bp long, and the same length appears in the headers of the source alignments. The .dict lines follow the SAM header format: @SQ lines with SN (name), LN (length), M5 (MD5 of the sequence), and the file, assembly and species (UR, AS, SP).

    With the index, samtools faidx extracts any region without reading the whole 3.1 GB file. Load samtools with its explicit version (the workshop pins every tool version; see the setup page):

    BASH 

    module load biocontainers
module load samtools/1.22.1
samtools faidx ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa chr20:88098-88118

    OUTPUT 

    >chr20:88098-88118
ATTTCATTGTTGTGTCCTATT

    The first line is a message the biocontainers module prints when it is loaded; the region follows as a short FASTA record. The region is 21 bases: samtools faidx regions are 1-based and include both ends (samtools faidx manual). Base 88,108, a T, sits in the middle. Remember this position; the child is heterozygous there, and we will come back to it in Episodes 4 and 5A.

    Step 4: Coordinate systems

    Genomic files count positions in two different ways:

    • 1-based, closed (VCF, SAM, samtools regions such as chr20:88098-88118): the first base of a chromosome is 1, and a range includes both its start and its end.
    • 0-based, half-open (BED): the first base is 0, the start is included, and the end is not. The BED interval chr20 88107 88108 is one base long: base 88,108 in 1-based coordinates (UCSC BED format).

    To convert a BED interval to 1-based coordinates, add 1 to the start and keep the end. The length of a BED interval is simply end minus start.

    The benchmark regions we use in Episode 6 are BED files. Look at the first lines of the one for HG002:

    BASH 

    head -3 resources/truth/HG002_v4.2.1_chr20.bed

    OUTPUT 

    chr20	81335	101267
chr20	101308	102558
chr20	102684	105312
    Challenge

    Challenge: convert coordinates

    1. Write the first interval of HG002_v4.2.1_chr20.bed as a 1-based samtools region. How many bases does it cover?
    2. A VCF record has POS 1000 and REF CAT, a deletion of AT. Which bases does REF span, in 1-based coordinates? Write the same span as a BED line.
    3. Write the region we extracted with samtools faidx (chr20:88098-88118) as a BED line.
    1. The first line is chr20 81335 101267. Add 1 to the start and keep the end: chr20:81336-101267. Its length is end minus start of the BED line: 101267 - 81335 = 19,932 bp.
    2. REF spans bases 1000 to 1002 (three bases, C, A, T). As BED: chr20 999 1002.
    3. chr20 88097 88118: subtract 1 from the start, keep the end. The length is 88118 - 88097 = 21, as before.

    Off-by-one errors are among the most common bugs in genomics scripts. When a tool accepts both formats, check which one it expects.

    Step 5: What a FASTQ record looks like

    Each read in a FASTQ file takes four lines: a name, the sequence, a + separator, and one quality character per base.

    BASH 

    zcat data/HG002_R1.fastq.gz | head -4

    OUTPUT 

    @A00744:46:HV3C3DSXX:2:1654:24334:32456
GACTGGGGAATTATGAGTTCCCTGTACCAACAGCGGAATGGGCTTTTCCCCACAGAGTGACATACTCCATCAGGAAAAAGAAAATGGAATTTACAACACAAACTTTCAAATAATTTGTGATGGAATGGGGAACAGAAACTAAGGCTCACAT
+
FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:F

    The first line is the read name; it records the instrument, run, flow cell, lane, tile and cluster position. The fourth line encodes the base qualities: here mostly F, with a few : and ,. Episode 3 decodes it.

    The files are compressed with gzip (.gz). Later we meet BGZF, the block-compressed variant made by bgzip: it is still readable by zcat, but it also allows an index and random access, which BAM and indexed VCF files need. A VCF compressed with plain gzip cannot be indexed.

    Data responsibility

    Callout

    Public data here, controlled data at home

    The GIAB data are public. NIST allows copying and redistribution of its benchmark data with acknowledgment of NIST (Data Usage section of the GIAB v5.0q README), which is why a copy can sit on Depot for this workshop.

    Your own human sequencing data may be different. Data from patients or research participants often comes with consent limits, data use agreements, or legal protections, and may only be stored and analyzed on approved, access-controlled systems. Do not copy such data to scratch or to a shared workshop space just because the commands work there. Before you start, ask your data provider and RCAC (rcac-help@purdue.edu) where the data may be stored and processed.

    Downloading from the source (not run)

    Reference only: do not run these commands in the workshop. The downloads are more than 9 GB, and the staged copy already contains the results.

    The source alignments for the three samples:

    BASH 

    wget https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/case-study-testdata/HG002.novaseq.pcr-free.35x.dedup.grch38_no_alt.chr20.bam
wget https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/case-study-testdata/HG003.novaseq.pcr-free.35x.dedup.grch38_no_alt.chr20.bam
wget https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/case-study-testdata/HG004.novaseq.pcr-free.35x.dedup.grch38_no_alt.chr20.bam

    Each alignment was converted to paired FASTQ. samtools collate groups the two reads of a pair together, and samtools fastq writes them to two files; reads whose mate is missing go to /dev/null:

    BASH 

    module load biocontainers
module load samtools/1.22.1
samtools collate -u -O -T collate.tmp HG002.novaseq.pcr-free.35x.dedup.grch38_no_alt.chr20.bam \
  | samtools fastq -n -1 HG002_R1.fastq.gz -2 HG002_R2.fastq.gz -0 /dev/null -s /dev/null -

    The reference FASTA, its .fai index and the bwa index from NCBI:

    BASH 

    wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/001/405/GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38/seqs_for_alignment_pipelines.ucsc_ids/GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38_no_alt_analysis_set.fna.gz
wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/001/405/GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38/seqs_for_alignment_pipelines.ucsc_ids/GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38_no_alt_analysis_set.fna.fai
wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCA/000/001/405/GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38/seqs_for_alignment_pipelines.ucsc_ids/GCA_000001405.15_GRCh38_no_alt_analysis_set.fna.bwa_index.tar.gz

    The benchmark call sets come from the GIAB release directories, for example the HG002 v5.0q small-variant benchmark and its regions:

    BASH 

    wget https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ReferenceSamples/giab/release/AshkenazimTrio/HG002_NA24385_son/latest/HG002_GRCh38_v5.0q_smvar.vcf.gz
wget https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ReferenceSamples/giab/release/AshkenazimTrio/HG002_NA24385_son/latest/HG002_GRCh38_v5.0q_smvar.benchmark.bed

    The full list of sources, with sizes and checksums, is in data-prep/sources.tsv, and the preparation scripts are in data-prep/.

    Summary

    Key Points
    • The data are the GIAB Ashkenazi trio (HG002 child, HG003 father, HG004 mother): NovaSeq PCR-free 151 bp paired reads, about 40x on chromosome 20.
    • The reads were selected from chromosome 20 alignments, so mapping rate and coverage outside chromosome 20 are not realistic.
    • Check every copy with checksums (md5sum -c) before using it.
    • The sample sheet and the PED file record sample names, roles, sex and relationships; later steps depend on them being right.
    • The GRCh38 no-alt analysis set leaves out alt contigs and uses UCSC-style names (chr20); every file in an analysis must use the same assembly and sequence names.
    • BED is 0-based and half-open; VCF, SAM and samtools regions are 1-based and closed.
    • Public reference data can be shared; your own human data may need an approved, controlled system.

    Content from 3. Read quality control

    Last updated on 2026-10-11 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do we tell whether the sequencing reads are good enough to call variants?
    • Do these reads need trimming before alignment?

    Objectives

    • Run FastQC and MultiQC in an interactive job.
    • Interpret base quality, adapter content, duplication and GC.
    • Decide whether trimming is needed before local alignment.

    Introduction

    Before aligning, we check that the reads are what we expect: the right length, good base qualities, few adapters, and nothing strange in their composition. FastQC writes one report per FASTQ file, and MultiQC combines all of them into one page so the samples can be compared side by side.

    For variant calling, read QC answers one practical question: is anything wrong with the reads that alignment and calling will not handle by themselves? With modern Illumina data the answer is usually no, and the main risk is the opposite one: removing good data because a QC plot looks unfamiliar.

    Prerequisite

    Before you start

    You need the workshop copy from the setup page and Episode 2 ($SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/data/ with six FASTQ files).

    Phred scores and binned qualities

    The fourth line of each FASTQ record (Episode 2) holds one character per base. Each character encodes the base quality as a Phred score: subtract 33 from the character’s ASCII code (SAM specification, which uses the same encoding). A Phred score Q means an estimated error probability of 10^(-Q/10).

    Our NovaSeq reads use only four different quality values, a scheme called quality binning. In the first 200,000 reads of the source data we found exactly these characters (feasibility memo):

    Character ASCII code Phred score Estimated error probability
    # 35 2 0.63
    , 44 11 0.08
    : 58 25 0.003
    F 70 37 0.0002
    Callout

    Why base quality matters for variant calling

    The caller uses base qualities directly. In the genotype likelihoods of Episode 1, a mismatching base with Q37 counts as strong evidence for an ALT allele, and a mismatching base with Q2 counts as almost none. bcftools also adjusts base qualities near indels before calling (base alignment quality, BAQ), so that mismatches caused by misaligned indels count less (bcftools manual, mpileup). Low-quality bases do not need to be removed for calling to work; they need to be reported honestly, and that is what the quality string does.

    Step 1: Run FastQC in an interactive session

    FastQC reads every base of every file, which is too much work for a login node. Start an interactive session on a compute node with 4 cores, then run FastQC on all six files, 4 at a time (-t 4):

    BASH 

    sinteractive -A rcac -q standby -p cpu -N 1 -n 4 --time=1:00:00
module load biocontainers
module load fastqc/0.12.1
module load multiqc/1.23
cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
fastqc -t 4 -o results/qc data/*.fastq.gz

    Starting the session can take a few minutes when the standby queue is busy. FastQC prints its progress for each file; in the workshop’s test run, FastQC and MultiQC together took about 4 minutes on 4 cores.

    Step 2: Combine the reports with MultiQC

    In the same session, run MultiQC on the FastQC output folder and list what was written:

    BASH 

    multiqc -o results/qc results/qc
ls results/qc

    OUTPUT 

           file_search | Search path: /scratch/negishi/aseethar/varcall-kit/kit-runs/kit-2026-10-11/scratch/varcall-workshop/results/qc
            fastqc | Found 6 reports
     write_results | Data        : results/qc/multiqc_data
     write_results | Report      : results/qc/multiqc_report.html
           multiqc | MultiQC complete
HG002_R1_fastqc.html
HG002_R1_fastqc.zip
HG002_R2_fastqc.html
HG002_R2_fastqc.zip
HG003_R1_fastqc.html
HG003_R1_fastqc.zip
HG003_R2_fastqc.html
HG003_R2_fastqc.zip
HG004_R1_fastqc.html
HG004_R1_fastqc.zip
HG004_R2_fastqc.html
HG004_R2_fastqc.zip
multiqc_data
multiqc_report.html

    MultiQC reports what it found (six FastQC reports) and where it wrote its output. The listing shows one _fastqc.html report and one _fastqc.zip archive per FASTQ file, plus multiqc_report.html and its data folder multiqc_data/.

    Type exit to leave the interactive session when you are done. To read the report, copy results/qc/multiqc_report.html to your computer (for example with scp, or the file browser in MobaXterm) and open it in a web browser.

    Callout

    Short on time?

    If your FastQC session did not finish, the completed reports are in the results copy. Open the MultiQC report from there instead of your own:

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/qc/multiqc_report.html $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/qc/

    Nothing later in the workshop reads the QC reports, so you can continue with Episode 4 either way.

    Step 3: Read the report

    FastQC marks each module with a pass, warning or fail. These marks come from thresholds designed for a generic whole-genome library (FastQC documentation); read the plots, not only the colors. Below, each module is described with what to expect from this dataset, followed by a schematic cartoon that shows what a problem looks like. The cartoons are not this workshop’s data.

    Per base sequence quality

    The distribution of base qualities at each position along the read. With binned qualities, the box plots in each FastQC report look blocky: medians, quartiles and percentiles can only take the four values (2, 11, 25, 37). That is binning, not a failure. In our files the median and both quartiles are 37 at every position; only the 10th percentile drops to 25 near the end of the read. MultiQC plots the mean, which stays near 35 to 36 and falls slightly over the last cycles.

    Per sequence quality scores

    The mean quality of each read, as a histogram. A good run has one sharp peak at high quality.

    Per sequence GC content

    The GC fraction of each read, compared with a theoretical distribution. Two separate peaks, or a sharp spike, can mean contamination from another organism or an overrepresented sequence. FastQC warns when the curve departs from the smooth normal shape it expects. Our six files peak near 40% GC with a shoulder near 50%, and FastQC warns for all six. The curves are the same in every file, which points to the composition of the sequenced region (all reads come from chromosome 20) rather than to contamination, which would differ between samples or add a separate peak.

    Per base N content

    The fraction of bases the sequencer could not call (N) at each position. It should be near zero everywhere.

    Sequence duplication levels

    How many reads have exactly the same sequence as another read. FastQC estimates this from the first reads of each file and from read 1 or read 2 alone, so it is only a rough guide. The duplicate rate that matters for calling is measured after alignment, from read pairs, in Episode 4.

    Duplicates have two main sources: PCR amplification during library preparation, and the sequencer itself, when one DNA fragment is read in more than one cluster (optical duplicates; the samtools markdup manual describes how they are detected). Our libraries are PCR-free, which removes most of the first kind, but not the second.

    Adapter content

    The fraction of reads that contain adapter sequence at each position. Adapters appear when a DNA fragment is shorter than the read length, so the sequencer reads past the end of the fragment into the adapter. Our fragments average about 400 bp (the insert sizes of the source alignments were 399.5 to 417.9 bp on average; feasibility memo), well above the 151 bp read length, so few reads should reach the adapter. FastQC 0.12 also counts poly-A and poly-G stretches in this module, and reports each adapter type as its own line.

    Challenge

    Challenge: interpret the QC report

    Using your MultiQC report (or the one from the results copy):

    1. How many reads does each file have, and are R1 and R2 of each sample equal?
    2. Which FastQC modules are not marked “pass” in at least one file? For each, decide whether it points to a problem for variant calling.
    3. Is there enough adapter sequence to justify trimming?
    4. What does FastQC report for duplication, and how does that compare with the duplicate rate after alignment that Episode 4 reports?
    1. HG002 has 9,462,450 reads in R1 and in R2, HG003 9,480,040 and HG004 9,347,118. R1 and R2 of a sample must have the same number of reads, because each read pair contributes one read to each file.
    2. Only one module is not marked pass: Per sequence GC content, a warning in all six files. The curves have a shoulder near 50% GC and are identical across files, so this reflects the sequence of chromosome 20, not a problem with the libraries. It is not a reason to change anything for variant calling.
    3. No. Adapter Content passes in all six files. The Illumina Universal Adapter reaches at most 0.37% to 0.54% of reads per file, at the read end; the highest lines, 1.43% to 1.49%, are FastQC’s poly-A series. With fragments averaging about 400 bp and 151 bp reads, adapter read-through is rare, and the aligner handles the few reads that have it (next section). No trimming is needed.
    4. FastQC reports that 84.3% to 85.3% of reads would remain after removing duplicates (“Total Deduplicated Percentage”), so it estimates 14.7% to 15.7% duplicates per file. After alignment, samtools markdup flags 10.4% to 11.0% of the reads as duplicates (Episode 4). The two numbers measure different things: FastQC compares single reads by sequence, markdup compares read pairs by alignment position.

    Step 4: Decide whether to trim

    Trimming removes adapter sequence and low-quality ends from reads before alignment. For variant calling with bwa mem, it is usually unnecessary:

    • bwa mem performs local alignment. It aligns the part of a read that matches the genome and soft-clips the rest: the clipped bases stay in the file but are not aligned and do not count as mismatches (bwa manual). Adapter sequence at a read end is clipped this way.
    • Base qualities already carry the uncertainty. The caller down-weights low-quality bases (callout above), so cutting them off gains little.
    • Trimming has costs. Shorter reads map less uniquely, uneven trimming creates differences between samples, and it adds parameters that must be recorded to reproduce the analysis.

    Trim when QC shows a real problem that the aligner cannot absorb: many short inserts with adapter in a large fraction of reads, a failed stretch of cycles, or a library type that needs it (for example, some amplicon and small-RNA protocols).

    Discussion

    Discussion: when would you trim?

    Your own data shows adapter content rising to 30% of reads at the 3’ end, and a median insert size of 120 bp with 150 bp reads. Would you trim before running bwa mem? What would you check after alignment to confirm your choice?

    Optional reference: not part of the hands-on, and not tested by the workshop’s run kit. If your data does need trimming, fastp detects and removes adapters, trims low-quality ends, keeps read pairs in sync and writes a QC report:

    BASH 

    module load biocontainers
module load fastp/0.23.2
fastp \
  -i sample_R1.fastq.gz \
  -I sample_R2.fastq.gz \
  -o sample_R1.trimmed.fastq.gz \
  -O sample_R2.trimmed.fastq.gz \
  --detect_adapter_for_pe \
  --thread 8 \
  --html sample.fastp.html \
  --json sample.fastp.json

    Run it in a batch job or an interactive session, never on a login node. Rerun FastQC on the trimmed files, and record the fastp version and options with your results.

    Summary

    Key Points
    • Base qualities are Phred scores; our NovaSeq reads use only four binned values (2, 11, 25, 37), which makes quality plots look blocky without indicating a problem.
    • FastQC and MultiQC summarize read quality; run them in an interactive job, not on a login node.
    • Pass, warn and fail marks come from generic thresholds; interpret each plot for your data type.
    • The caller uses base qualities directly, so low-quality bases are down-weighted rather than removed.
    • bwa mem soft-clips adapters and poor read ends, so trimming is usually unnecessary for these data.

    Content from 4. Read alignment and alignment QC

    Last updated on 2026-10-11 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 90 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How are reads placed on the reference genome?
    • Why does mapping quality matter for variant calling?
    • How do we produce analysis-ready BAM files on the cluster?
    • How do we know the alignment worked?

    Objectives

    • Explain why mapping quality matters for calling.
    • Align with bwa mem using correct read groups.
    • Produce sorted, duplicate-marked and indexed BAMs.
    • Read SAM fields (FLAG, CIGAR, MAPQ).
    • Interpret mapping, pairing, duplicate, insert-size and coverage metrics.
    • View a locus.

    Introduction

    A caller can only be as good as the alignments it reads. In this episode we align the reads of all three samples to GRCh38 with bwa mem, mark duplicate reads, and write sorted, indexed BAM files. Then we check the alignments: how many reads mapped, how many in proper pairs, how many duplicates, how deep the coverage is, and what the reads look like at one variant.

    Alignment is the longest job of the day, so we start it first and take the script apart while it runs.

    Prerequisite

    Before you start

    You need the workshop copy from Episode 2: the FASTQ files in data/, the sample sheet data/samples.tsv, the reference links in ref/, and the script scripts/align.sh. Episode 3 is not required.

    Step 1: Submit the alignment job

    The alignment script is already in your scripts/ folder. Submit it now from that folder; the next sections explain every line while it runs:

    BASH 

    cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/scripts
sbatch align.sh

    sbatch prints a job ID. The script is an array job with three tasks, one per sample, and each task uses 16 cores. In the workshop’s test runs each task took 10 to 14 minutes, plus the time waiting in the standby queue. Check on it with:

    BASH 

    squeue -u $USER

    Each task writes its log to scripts/cluster-align.<jobid>.out and .err. When squeue no longer lists the job, it has finished.

    Pacing (plan section 4): have learners submit align.sh at the end of the Episode 2-3 block, before the morning break, so the jobs run during the break. Episode 4 then dissects the script while the jobs finish. If learners submit only now, the explanation sections below still cover the run time.

    Callout

    Short on time?

    If your alignment job fails or is still waiting when we reach Step 3, copy the finished BAM files, their indexes and the duplicate statistics from the results copy into your own results/bam/ (about 3.2 GB):

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/bam/HG00?.markdup.bam* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/bam/
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/bam/HG00?.markdup.stats.txt $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/bam/

    Cancel your own job first (scancel <jobid>), so it does not overwrite the copies. Episodes 5A onward work the same with either set of BAMs.

    How short-read alignment works

    An aligner has to find, for each of millions of reads, the place in a 3.1 Gb genome where it fits best, allowing for sequencing errors and real variants. Checking every position for every read would take far too long, so bwa mem uses seed and extend: it first finds exact matches between the read and the genome (seeds) using an index of the reference, and then extends the best seeds into a full alignment that may contain mismatches and gaps (bwa manual).

    bwa mem aligns locally: if the end of a read does not match, for example because it runs into adapter sequence or crosses a structural variant, that end is soft-clipped, kept in the file but not aligned. With paired reads, it also uses the expected distance and orientation of the two mates to choose between candidate positions and to rescue a mate that did not align well on its own.

    Mapping quality and multi-mapping reads

    Some reads fit equally well in several places, for example inside a repeat. The aligner then picks one of the equally good positions and reports how unsure it is as the mapping quality (MAPQ): the Phred-scaled probability that the position is wrong (SAM specification). A read with several equally good positions gets MAPQ 0: the position written in the file is one guess among them.

    This is why mapping quality matters for calling. If a read from one copy of a repeat is placed on another copy, every difference between the two copies looks like a variant at the wrong place. Callers down-weight or skip low-MAPQ reads, and Episode 6 filters sites whose reads have low average mapping quality.

    The reference index

    bwa mem needs the reference in its own index format: the five files GRCh38_no_alt.fa.amb, .ann, .bwt, .pac and .sa in ref/. NCBI publishes this index for the no-alt analysis set, and it loads in bwa 0.7.17, so we did not build it (feasibility memo). Unpacked, it is 5.42 GB.

    The index is loaded into memory by every alignment task. On Negishi, memory comes with the cores you request, about 1.9 GB per core; there is no separate memory request in our scripts. The 16 cores of each task bring enough memory for the index and the sorting step: in the reference run, the largest task used 13.5 GiB.

    Reference only: do not run this on the workshop reference.

    For your own organism, build the index once from its FASTA file, in a batch job, and keep it with the reference:

    BASH 

    module load biocontainers
module load bwa/0.7.17
bwa index my_genome.fa

    This writes the same five files next to my_genome.fa. For a genome the size of human it is a long, memory-hungry job, which is why we use the published index. Index files only work with the FASTA they were built from: if you change the FASTA (for example, rename a sequence), build the index again.

    Step 2: The alignment script, line by line

    This is scripts/align.sh as you submitted it:

    BASH 

    #!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --account=rcac
#SBATCH --qos=standby
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --job-name=align
#SBATCH --array=1-3
#SBATCH --output=cluster-%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=cluster-%x.%j.err

module load biocontainers
module load bwa/0.7.17
module load samtools/1.22.1

WORK=$SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
REF=$WORK/ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa
OUTDIR=$WORK/results/bam
mkdir -p $OUTDIR

# One sample per array task: task N reads line N+1 of samples.tsv (line 1 is the header)
LINE=$(sed -n "$((SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID + 1))p" $WORK/data/samples.tsv)
IFS=$'\t' read -r SAMPLE ROLE SEX FAMILY FASTQ_R1 FASTQ_R2 RG_ID RG_LB RG_PL <<< "$LINE"

# Read group: SM becomes the sample name in the VCF. Keep \t as typed; bwa turns it into tabs.
RG="@RG\tID:${RG_ID}\tSM:${SAMPLE}\tLB:${RG_LB}\tPL:${RG_PL}"

# -K 100000000 makes the alignments identical for any number of threads
bwa mem -K 100000000 -t $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK -R "$RG" $REF \
    $WORK/data/$FASTQ_R1 $WORK/data/$FASTQ_R2 \
  | samtools fixmate -m -u - - \
  | samtools sort -u -@ 4 -m 1500M -T $OUTDIR/${SAMPLE}.sorttmp - \
  | samtools markdup -@ 4 --write-index -f $OUTDIR/${SAMPLE}.markdup.stats.txt \
      -T $OUTDIR/${SAMPLE}.mdtmp - $OUTDIR/${SAMPLE}.markdup.bam

    The SLURM header

    The #SBATCH lines request one node, 16 cores (--cpus-per-task=16) and one hour, on the cpu partition with the standby QoS, under the workshop account. --array=1-3 turns the script into three tasks, numbered 1, 2 and 3, that run independently; inside each task, $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID holds its number. Logs go to cluster-<jobname>.<jobid>.out and .err in the folder you submitted from.

    One sample per task

    sed -n "$((SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID + 1))p" prints one line of samples.tsv: line 2 for task 1, because line 1 is the header. IFS=$'\t' read -r ... then splits that line at tabs into named variables, one per column. Task 1 aligns the first sample in the sheet, task 2 the second, and so on, so the sheet decides which sample each task processes.

    The path to the sheet is absolute ($WORK/data/samples.tsv). A script that reads samples.tsv relative to the current folder works only when it is submitted from the folder that contains the sheet, and fails, or reads the wrong file, from anywhere else.

    Read groups

    A read group labels a set of reads that were sequenced together. bwa mem -R adds a header line (@RG) to the BAM file and tags every read with its ID. The fields we set are defined in the SAM specification:

    Field Meaning Value here
    ID unique identifier of the read group rg_id from the sample sheet
    SM sample name the sample, for example HG002
    LB library rg_lb from the sample sheet
    PL sequencing platform ILLUMINA

    SM matters most: bcftools takes the sample names of the VCF from the SM field of the read groups, so every BAM must carry the right one. Reads with the same SM are treated as one sample, even if they are in different files.

    The \t in the RG= line is typed as a backslash and a t, not as a real tab. bwa converts each \t into a tab when it writes the header. Real tab characters in the -R argument, or a missing ID or SM, make bwa stop with an error.

    bwa mem

    • -K 100000000 makes bwa mem process input in batches of a fixed size (100 million bases) regardless of the number of threads. Without it, the batch size depends on the thread count, and so can the results (bwa manual). The reference run checked this: HG002 aligned at 16 and at 32 cores gave identical alignments.
    • -t $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK uses all 16 cores of the task.
    • The output is SAM text, written to standard output and piped (|) straight into the next command. No large intermediate file is written.

    samtools fixmate -m, then sort, then markdup

    The three samtools steps follow the order the samtools markdup manual requires:

    1. samtools fixmate -m fills in information about each read’s mate, including the mate score tag that markdup needs (added by -m). It must see the two reads of a pair next to each other. bwa mem writes pairs together, so its output can go straight into fixmate; a coordinate-sorted file would first need samtools collate.
    2. samtools sort sorts by position on the genome, which callers and viewers need. -@ 4 adds 4 threads, -m 1500M lets each thread use up to 1.5 GB of memory before writing temporary files, and -T names those temporary files.
    3. samtools markdup finds duplicates in the sorted file, flags them, writes the final BAM, and, with --write-index, its index. -f writes a short statistics file.

    -u passes uncompressed data between the steps, which saves the time of compressing and decompressing data that is read again immediately. The - arguments mean standard input or standard output. Sorting before fixmate is a common mistake: fixmate needs the two reads of each pair next to each other, and in a position-sorted file it cannot pair them, so the mate information markdup relies on is missing or wrong.

    Callout

    Why mark duplicates, and why not remove them?

    Duplicates are copies of one original DNA fragment. If one fragment carries a sequencing error and is read several times, the error appears in several reads and looks like independent support for a variant. Marking duplicates lets the caller count each fragment once.

    samtools markdup flags duplicates (FLAG bit 1024) and keeps them in the file. bcftools skips flagged duplicates by default (bcftools manual, mpileup), and the reads are still there if you need them, for example to inspect a site or recount. The old samtools rmdup command removes reads instead; use markdup (samtools manual).

    Challenge

    Challenge: what if the read groups are wrong?

    1. Suppose samples.tsv listed HG002 in the sample column of all three rows. The script would still run without error. What would the VCF in Episode 5A look like?
    2. Why does the script write the read group from the sample sheet instead of having you type it for each sample?
    1. All three BAMs would carry SM:HG002, so bcftools would treat all reads as one sample. The VCF would have one sample column, HG002, with the reads of three people pooled: about 116x of mixed evidence and genotypes that belong to nobody. Nothing would fail, which is what makes this error dangerous. Check the @RG lines after alignment (Step 3 does).
    2. One source of truth: the sample name, file names and read group come from the same row, so they cannot disagree, and the sheet is a record of what was done. Typing them per sample is where mistakes come from.

    SAM and BAM

    The aligner writes SAM, a tab-separated text format with a header (lines starting with @) and one line per alignment. BAM is the same content, compressed in blocks so it can be indexed for fast access to any region; that is what we keep. CRAM compresses further by storing only differences from the reference, and so needs the exact reference FASTA to be read back (htslib file formats).

    Each alignment line has 11 mandatory columns (SAM specification):

    Column Name Meaning
    1 QNAME read name (both reads of a pair share it)
    2 FLAG properties of the read, as a sum of bit values
    3 RNAME reference sequence name, for example chr20
    4 POS 1-based position of the leftmost aligned base
    5 MAPQ mapping quality
    6 CIGAR how the read aligns: M aligned (match or mismatch), I insertion, D deletion, S soft clip, H hard clip
    7 RNEXT reference name of the mate (= for the same)
    8 PNEXT position of the mate
    9 TLEN observed template (fragment) length
    10 SEQ read sequence
    11 QUAL base qualities, as in FASTQ

    For example, the CIGAR 100M2D51M means 100 aligned bases, a 2 bp deletion in the read relative to the reference, then 51 aligned bases. 20S131M means the first 20 bases are soft-clipped.

    The FLAG is a sum of bits, each with a meaning. The ones you meet most often:

    Bit Meaning
    1 read is paired
    2 read is in a proper pair
    4 read is unmapped
    16 read is reverse-complemented
    32 mate is reverse-complemented
    64 first read of the pair
    128 second read of the pair
    256 secondary alignment
    1024 duplicate
    2048 supplementary alignment

    Step 3: Check the alignments

    When squeue shows that your alignment job has finished, start an interactive session and load the QC tools. List the output files first:

    BASH 

    sinteractive -A rcac -q standby -p cpu -N 1 -n 4 --time=1:00:00
module load biocontainers
module load samtools/1.22.1
module load mosdepth/0.3.3
module load multiqc/1.23
cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
ls -lh results/bam

    OUTPUT 

    total 3.1G
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop  1.1G Oct 10 21:35 HG002.markdup.bam
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop  249K Oct 10 21:35 HG002.markdup.bam.csi
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop   769 Oct 10 21:35 HG002.markdup.stats.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop  1.1G Oct 10 21:32 HG003.markdup.bam
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop  248K Oct 10 21:32 HG003.markdup.bam.csi
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop   770 Oct 10 21:32 HG003.markdup.stats.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop 1015M Oct 10 21:31 HG004.markdup.bam
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop  247K Oct 10 21:31 HG004.markdup.bam.csi
-rw-r--r-- 1 aseethar workshop   769 Oct 10 21:31 HG004.markdup.stats.txt

    The first two lines are the message the biocontainers module prints when it is loaded. Each sample has a BAM file (about 1 GB), its .csi index and the duplicate statistics from markdup. samtools markdup --write-index writes a CSI index rather than the older .bai format; samtools, bcftools and mosdepth read both.

    Now compute three sets of metrics for each sample: samtools flagstat (counts by FLAG), samtools stats (detailed statistics) and mosdepth (coverage). This takes about 3 minutes for the three samples:

    BASH 

    for SAMPLE in HG002 HG003 HG004; do
    samtools flagstat -@ 4 results/bam/$SAMPLE.markdup.bam > results/qc_alignment/$SAMPLE.flagstat.txt
    samtools stats -@ 4 results/bam/$SAMPLE.markdup.bam > results/qc_alignment/$SAMPLE.stats.txt
    mosdepth -t 4 -n --fast-mode -c chr20 results/qc_alignment/$SAMPLE results/bam/$SAMPLE.markdup.bam
done

    For mosdepth, -c chr20 restricts the calculation to chromosome 20, -n skips the per-base output file, and --fast-mode skips the correction for overlapping mates and the details of each CIGAR, which the mosdepth documentation recommends for most uses.

    Callout

    Short on time?

    If the metrics are not ready, copy them from the results copy:

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/qc_alignment/HG00?.* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/qc_alignment/

    Read counts by flag

    BASH 

    cat results/qc_alignment/HG002.flagstat.txt

    OUTPUT 

    18980761 + 0 in total (QC-passed reads + QC-failed reads)
18924900 + 0 primary
0 + 0 secondary
55861 + 0 supplementary
1975897 + 0 duplicates
1975897 + 0 primary duplicates
18944359 + 0 mapped (99.81% : N/A)
18888498 + 0 primary mapped (99.81% : N/A)
18924900 + 0 paired in sequencing
9462450 + 0 read1
9462450 + 0 read2
18759278 + 0 properly paired (99.12% : N/A)
18852096 + 0 with itself and mate mapped
36402 + 0 singletons (0.19% : N/A)
6198 + 0 with mate mapped to a different chr
1177 + 0 with mate mapped to a different chr (mapQ>=5)

    Each line counts reads that pass QC and reads that fail it (always 0 here). “primary” counts each read once (18,924,900, the same as the FASTQ files); the total also includes 55,861 supplementary alignments, the extra records written when parts of one read align to different places. “singletons” are the 36,402 reads whose mate did not map.

    Detailed statistics

    The SN (summary numbers) section of samtools stats holds most of what we need:

    grep ^SN results/qc_alignment/HG002.stats.txt | cut -f2- | head -40

    The lines to read first: raw total sequences (reads in the file), reads mapped, reads properly paired, reads duplicated, reads MQ0 (mapped reads with mapping quality 0), insert size average and error rate (mismatches per aligned base, which includes real variants).

    Coverage

    BASH 

    cat results/qc_alignment/HG002.mosdepth.summary.txt

    OUTPUT 

    chrom	length	bases	mean	min	max
chr20	64444167	2518794994	39.08	0	13784
total	64444167	2518794994	39.08	0	13784

    The columns are the chromosome, its length, the number of aligned bases counted, and the mean, minimum and maximum depth. The total row repeats chr20 because we restricted the calculation to it.

    The mean is only a summary. results/qc_alignment/HG002.mosdepth.global.dist.txt lists, for each depth, the fraction of chromosome 20 covered at least that deeply, which shows how uniform the coverage is. The MultiQC report below plots it.

    Mapping quality 0 and read groups

    Count the reads with mapping quality 0, and check the read group the script wrote:

    BASH 

    samtools view -c -e 'mapq==0' results/bam/HG002.markdup.bam
samtools view -H results/bam/HG002.markdup.bam | grep '^@RG'

    OUTPUT 

    1054357
@RG	ID:HG002.pcr-free	SM:HG002	LB:HG002.pcr-free	PL:ILLUMINA

    -e 'mapq==0' is a filter expression: samtools view keeps only records for which it is true, and -c counts them instead of printing them (samtools view manual).

    Summarize with MultiQC

    MultiQC finds the flagstat, stats and mosdepth outputs and puts all samples side by side:

    BASH 

    multiqc -o results/qc_alignment results/qc_alignment results/bam

    Copy results/qc_alignment/multiqc_report.html to your computer and open it, as in Episode 3.

    Challenge

    Challenge: interpret the alignment metrics

    Using the samtools stats output and the MultiQC report:

    1. What fraction of HG002’s reads mapped, and what fraction are in proper pairs? Would you expect the same in a real whole-genome run?
    2. What fraction of reads are marked as duplicates in each sample?
    3. What is the average insert size, and how does it compare with the read length?
    4. What is the mean depth on chromosome 20 in each sample, and what fraction of chromosome 20 is covered by at least 10 reads in HG002?
    1. HG002 has 18,924,900 reads; 18,888,498 mapped (99.81%) and 18,759,278 are properly paired (99.12%). HG003 and HG004 are similar (99.77% and 99.82% mapped). In a real whole-genome run you would not see this: our reads were selected because they aligned to chromosome 20 before (Episode 2), so nearly all of them align again.
    2. HG002 10.44% (1,975,897 reads), HG003 10.98% (2,082,305), HG004 10.99% (2,053,967). PCR-free libraries still have duplicates (Episode 3). They stay in the files, flagged, and the caller skips them.
    3. The average insert size is 410.1 bp in HG002, 417.8 bp in HG003 and 399.4 bp in HG004, with standard deviations of 162 to 173 bp. The fragments are longer than two reads (2 x 151 = 302 bp), so the two reads of most pairs do not overlap, and adapter read-through is rare (Episode 3).
    4. Mean depth: HG002 39.08x, HG003 38.90x, HG004 38.42x. In HG002, 98.0% of chromosome 20 is covered by at least 10 reads. Part of the rest is sequence that no read can cover: chromosome 20 contains stretches of N in the reference.
    Challenge

    Challenge: how many reads have mapping quality 0?

    1. How many of HG002’s reads have mapping quality 0, as a fraction of all reads? Compare the count from samtools view -c -e 'mapq==0' with reads MQ0 from samtools stats.
    2. Where in the genome do you expect these reads?
    3. Why should a caller give these reads little or no weight?
    1. samtools stats reports 983,436 mapped reads with MAPQ 0 in HG002, 5.20% of 18,924,900 reads (HG003 5.28%, HG004 4.82%). samtools view -c counted 1,054,357, which is 70,921 more. samtools stats counts only mapped reads (its comment says “mapped and MQ=0”) and leaves out supplementary alignments, while samtools view -c counts every record whose MAPQ is 0. The 36,402 unmapped reads also have MAPQ 0 in the file, and supplementary records (55,861 in all) can account for the rest.
    2. In repeats and duplicated sequence: segmental duplications, the centromere, and other regions where a 151 bp read, or even a read pair, matches several places equally well.
    3. A MAPQ 0 read may come from another copy of the repeat. Differences between the copies would look like variants. Episode 6 shows that the raw calls in the centromere have a much lower transition/transversion ratio than calls elsewhere, the signature of many false calls.

    Step 4: Read individual alignments

    Look at a few alignments at the heterozygous site from Episode 2, chr20:88,108. samtools view with a region prints the reads overlapping it; we cut the output to the first nine columns, leaving out the sequence and qualities:

    BASH 

    samtools view results/bam/HG002.markdup.bam chr20:88108-88108 | head -3 | cut -f1-9

    OUTPUT 

    A00744:46:HV3C3DSXX:2:1441:32533:3443	163	chr20	87958	60	151M	=	88080	273
A00744:46:HV3C3DSXX:2:2505:30581:31125	1171	chr20	87961	60	151M	=	87802	-310
A00744:46:HV3C3DSXX:2:2505:29134:25895	147	chr20	87961	60	151M	=	87802	-310

    samtools flags translates FLAG values into names (samtools flags manual):

    BASH 

    samtools flags 99 1123

    OUTPUT 

    0x63	99	PAIRED,PROPER_PAIR,MREVERSE,READ1
0x463	1123	PAIRED,PROPER_PAIR,MREVERSE,READ1,DUP
    Challenge

    Challenge: decode a FLAG

    1. Decode FLAG 99 by hand with the bit table above. Which read of the pair is it, on which strand, and is the pair proper?
    2. FLAG 1123 differs from 99 by one bit. Which one, and what does it mean for variant calling?
    3. Pick one read from the samtools view output above and decode its FLAG and CIGAR.
    1. 99 = 64 + 32 + 2 + 1: paired (1), in a proper pair (2), mate reverse-complemented (32), first read of the pair (64). Bit 16 is not set, so this read is on the forward strand and its mate on the reverse strand: the usual orientation of a proper Illumina pair.
    2. 1123 = 1024 + 99: the same read, marked as a duplicate. bcftools skips it when calling.
    3. In the output above, the first read has FLAG 163 = 128 + 32 + 2 + 1: the second read of a proper pair, on the forward strand, with its mate on the reverse strand. The second read has FLAG 1171 = 1024 + 128 + 16 + 2 + 1: the second read of a proper pair, on the reverse strand, marked as a duplicate. The third read (FLAG 147) has the same position, mate position and template length as the second, which is why markdup flagged one of the two. All three have the CIGAR 151M: all 151 bases aligned without gaps or clipping.

    Step 5: View a locus

    A text view of the pileup shows what the caller will see. samtools tview normally runs as an interactive full-screen viewer; with -d T it prints a text snapshot instead, -p sets the first position shown, -w the width in columns, and -i hides insertions, so that each column is one reference position (samtools tview manual). Starting 20 bases before chr20:88,108 puts the variant in column 21:

    Challenge

    Challenge: read the pileup

    1. In the text view, count the reads that show C (or c) in column 21, and the reads that match the reference there. What genotype do you expect the caller to report for HG002?
    2. The benchmark says HG002 is homozygous for the ALT allele A at chr20:85,259 (reference G). Write the tview command that shows this site in column 21, and predict what you will see before you run it.

    1. Column 21 holds 39 reads: 14 show C or c and 25 match the reference T, and the consensus line shows Y. That is 36% C, fewer than half, but not unusual for a heterozygous site: with 39 reads, a perfectly balanced site gives 14 or fewer reads of one particular allele about 5% of the time (binomial, Episode 1). Expect the caller to report 0/1. The benchmark for HG002 agrees: 0/1 at this position.

    2. Start 20 bases earlier, at 85,239:

      BASH 

      samtools tview -d T -i -w 41 -p chr20:85239 results/bam/HG002.markdup.bam ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa

      Nearly every read should show A or a in column 21, and the consensus line shows A: a homozygous ALT site. In the test run, all 50 reads in column 21 show A or a and none matches the reference G.

    Graphical viewing is decided in P6 (IGV through a graphical session, or prepared snapshots). Until then, samtools tview -d T is the locus view for this episode. Learners can also run samtools tview without -d T for the interactive viewer (? for help, q to quit).

    Base quality recalibration (concept only)

    Sequencers can be systematically over- or under-confident in their base qualities, for example in certain sequence contexts or late in a read. Base quality score recalibration (BQSR) in GATK models these errors from mismatches at positions that are not known variant sites, and rewrites the qualities (GATK documentation). It needs a database of known variants for the organism.

    We do not recalibrate in this workshop. bcftools does not require it, and many organisms have no database of known variants. GATK’s own pipeline uses it; Episode 5B, self-paced, discusses where it applies.

    Summary

    Key Points
    • bwa mem finds seeds with an index of the reference, extends them into local alignments, and soft-clips ends that do not match.
    • Mapping quality is the Phred-scaled probability that a read is placed wrongly; reads that fit several places equally well get MAPQ 0 and can create false variants.
    • Read groups label reads by sample; SM becomes the sample name in the VCF, so it must come from the sample sheet.
    • The order is bwa mem, samtools fixmate -m, samtools sort, samtools markdup; duplicates are flagged, not removed, and the caller skips them.
    • -K makes bwa mem results independent of the number of threads.
    • Check every alignment with flagstat, stats and mosdepth, and compare samples in MultiQC. Here about 99.8% of reads mapped, about 11% are duplicates, and mean depth is about 39x on chromosome 20.
